Flow past a cylinder · CPU vs GPU

HPC case study · computational fluid dynamics

One cylinder, two backends:
CPU vs GPU on an HPC cluster

I simulated the Kármán vortex street with the lattice-Boltzmann method, and ran the same code two ways on the Imperial HPC cluster: across 20 CPU cores with MPI, and on a single NVIDIA L40S GPU with JAX. Identical physics; the GPU ran about 40× faster.

The computed vorticity field — vortices shed alternately from the cylinder and drift downstream. Blue = clockwise, red = counter-clockwise.
Lattice-Boltzmann (D2Q9, BGK)NumPy · mpi4py · JAXImperial CX3 · PBS ProRe = 200

The Kármán vortex street

Above a critical speed, the wake behind a cylinder becomes unstable and sheds vortices alternately from top and bottom — a self-sustaining, periodic vortex street. It is why flagpoles hum and chimneys get spiral strakes. Two dimensionless numbers govern it:

Re = U·D / ν   ·   St = f·D / U Reynolds number (inertia vs viscosity) sets the regime; the Strouhal number is the dimensionless shedding frequency — remarkably, St ≈ 0.2 across a huge range of Re

This run is at Re = 200, squarely in the clean periodic-shedding regime, and the measured Strouhal number comes out near the textbook ~0.2 — recovered from the simulation, not put in by hand.

Lattice-Boltzmann, not Navier–Stokes directly

Rather than discretising the Navier–Stokes equations directly (which needs a global pressure solve — awkward to parallelise), lattice-Boltzmann tracks populations of fictitious particles streaming along 9 discrete directions on a grid (the D2Q9 model). The whole time step is two local operations.

collide:  fi ← fi − ω (fi − fieq),   ω = 1/τ relax the populations toward local equilibrium — purely on-cell, no communication
fieq = wi ρ [ 1 + 3(ci·u) + 4.5(ci·u)² − 1.5|u|² ] the equilibrium distribution (a low-Mach expansion of Maxwell–Boltzmann)

Streaming, moments, and walls

stream:  fi(x + ci, t+1) = fiout(x, t) shift each population one cell along its direction — the only nearest-neighbour step

Density and velocity are simple moments of the nine populations, and the viscosity is set by the relaxation time:

ρ = Σi fi  ·  ρu = Σi ci fi  ·  ν = (τ − ½)/3

The cylinder is a no-slip wall via bounce-back (each population reflects straight back), with a Zou/He velocity inlet and an outflow boundary. The key structural fact: collision is local, streaming touches only an immediate neighbour — the stencil pattern that parallelises beautifully.

Distributed CPU: domain decomposition + halo exchange

The grid is cut into vertical strips, one per process (“rank”). Each rank computes its own strip; the only communication is a single ghost-column exchange with its neighbours each step, so streaming can carry populations across strip borders.

mpi4py 
# the one communication step, per time step
comm.Sendrecv(my_last_col,  dest=right, sendtag=11,
              recvbuf=ghostL, source=left,  recvtag=11)
comm.Sendrecv(my_first_col, dest=left,  sendtag=22,
              recvbuf=ghostR, source=right, recvtag=22)
# then stream locally inside each padded strip
Communication is tiny. Each rank exchanges one column (O(ny)) while computing over a whole strip (O(w·ny)). Verified bit-for-bit against a serial reference for 1–8 ranks before trusting the cluster. Run on 20 cores of one node (PBS medium queue).

Single GPU: jit + scan, the whole loop on-device

The same step, written once in NumPy-style JAX, is JIT-compiled and the entire time loop fused with lax.scan into a single GPU kernel. No manual parallelism — the compiler maps it across the GPU, and the whole lattice lives in device memory.

JAX 
@jax.jit
def step(f, vel, obst, omega):
    ...                         # collide + boundaries + stream
    return f

def body(f, _): return step(f, vel, obst, omega), None
f, _ = jax.lax.scan(body, f0, length=steps)  # fuse all steps
Same code, any accelerator. Matches the serial result to 2×10−15 (float64). Multi-GPU halo exchange is available via shard_map + ppermute. Run on one NVIDIA L40S (PBS gpu72 queue).

MPI and JAX are the same halo exchange

  CPU · MPI GPU · JAX
Parallelismexplicit ranks, you place each messagesharded arrays, compiler places it
Halo exchangeSendrecv of edge columnsppermute around a device ring
Scales to10⁵–10⁶ CPU coresmany accelerators (GPU/TPU)
Get the decomposition right once — local compute, exchange a thin halo — and the choice of CPU or GPU is a choice of tool, not of algorithm. The Sendrecv around a ring of ranks is the ppermute around a ring of devices.

Same physics, ~40× the speed

Both backends ran the identical problem — a 600×200 grid for 40,000 steps at Re = 200 — and produced the same flow (max|u| = 0.1008 in both).

Takeaways

  • The right algorithm scales. Lattice-Boltzmann is explicit and stencil-local, so it maps cleanly onto both distributed CPUs and a GPU — no global solves, minimal communication.
  • One GPU vs a CPU node. For this workload a single L40S replaced 20 CPU cores and finished ~40× sooner — the kind of throughput that changes what’s feasible to explore.
  • Portable and verified. The same physics core, two parallel strategies, each checked against a serial reference before trusting the cluster runs.
One thing to remember: local compute + a thin halo exchange turns a laptop fluid toy into a simulation that fills a supercomputer — and MPI and JAX are just two ways to say it.

Download it and run every version

Pure NumPy for the physics; mpi4py and JAX for the two parallel versions. The bundle includes the solvers, the production run scripts (which save the figures), the bit-for-bit decomposition check, and ready-to-use Imperial CX3 (PBS Pro) job scripts with a README of the exact cluster setup.

Quick start.  python3 lbm.py (serial) · mpiexec -n 20 python3 lbm_mpi_run.py (CPU) · python3 lbm_jax_run.py (GPU). The README has the full HPC recipe.
